'''Dalabon''' is a [[Gunwinyguan languages|Gunwinyguan language]] of [[Arnhem Land]], Australia. It is a severely [[Language endangerment|endangered]] language,<ref>{{Cite journal| last = Ponsonnet| first = Maïa| date = 2018| title = Expressivity and performance. Expressing compassion and grief with a prosodic contour in Gunwinyguan languages (northern Australia)| journal = Journal of Pragmatics| volume = 136| pages = 79–96| issn = 0378-2166| doi = 10.1016/j.pragma.2018.08.009| hdl = 1885/165435| s2cid = 149776540| hdl-access = free}}</ref> with perhaps as few as three fluent speakers remaining as of 2018.<ref name=Cutfield2018>{{Cite book| last = Cutfield| first = Sarah|editor= Stephen Levinson |editor2=Sarah Cutfield |editor3=Michael Dunn |editor4=Nick Enfield |editor5=Sergio Meira |editor6=David Wilkins | date = 2018-06-30| title = Demonstratives in Cross-Linguistic Perspective| chapter = Dalabon exophoric uses of demonstratives| publisher = Cambridge University Press| isbn = 978-1-108-34137-0| page = 92}}</ref>

-->Dalabon is also known as Dangbon (the [[Kune dialect|Kune]] or [[Mayali language|Mayali]] name), Ngalkbun (the [[Jawoyn language|Jawoyn]] name), and Buwan (the [[Rembarrnga language|Rembarrnga]] name).<ref name="AIATSIS"/>

==Classification==
Dalabon belongs to the [[Gunwinyguan languages]] branch of the [[Macro-Gunwinyguan|Arnhem languages]]; its nearest relatives are [[Kunwinjku]], [[Kune language|Kune]], [[Mayali]] (varieties often grouped together as Bininj Kunwok), and [[Kunbarlang language|Kunbarlang]]. Its next closest relatives are [[Rembarrnga language|Rembarrnga]], and other languages within the Gunwinyguan family, including [[Jawoyn]], [[Ngalakgan]], [[Ngandi]], [[Wubuy]], and [[Anindilyakwa language|Enindhilyakwa]].

== Official status ==
Dalabon has no official status. Local schools spent years holding sporadic programs teaching Dalabon, but these operations did not receive enough governmental support. Therefore, the condition of the programs is still vulnerable.

== Dialects ==
Given the limited number of Dalabon speakers, the study of dialects has become challenging to investigate. Speakers recall a distinction between two different types of speech, {{lang|ngk|dalabon-djurrkdjurrk}} ("fast." "lively") and {{lang|ngk|dalabon-murduk}} ("articulate"). However, no significant difference has been found between the two speeches.

===Phonotactics===
Like many Australian languages, Dalabon restricts the [[Voiced dental and alveolar trills|alveolar trill]] ''rr'' [r] from occurring word-initially.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Baker |first1=Brett |last2=Harvey |first2=Mark |title=The Phonology and Morphology of Australian Languages |date=2025 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=153}}</ref>

The [[glottal stop]] ''h'' [ʔ] is also restricted to occurring in syllable codas in Dalabon, as is the case for most Australian languages with this segment;<ref>{{cite book |last1=Baker |first1=Brett |last2=Harvey |first2=Mark |title=The Phonology and Morphology of Australian Languages |date=2025 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=122–123}}</ref> however, the glottal stop is also permitted within prosodic words rather than restricted to their right edge. 

[[Fortis and lenis#Consonant length|Long (or fortis) stops]] are characteristically limited to word-medial position<ref>{{cite book |last1=Evans |first1=Nicholas |last2=Merlan |first2=Francesca |last3=Tukumba |first3=Maggie |title=A First Dictionary of Dalabon |date=2004 |publisher=Maningrida Arts and Culture |page=xxii}}</ref>, just as they are in other Central Arnhem languages featuring a fortis/lenis (or short/long) stop contrast.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Baker |first1=Brett |last2=Harvey |first2=Mark |title=The Phonology and Morphology of Australian Languages |date=2025 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=117}}</ref>

The syllable structure of Dalabon is CV(C)(C)(C), or more specifically:

CV(L)(N)(h) ''or'' CV(L)(S)

where:
*L is a [[liquid consonant]] ([[lateral consonant|lateral]] or [[rhotic consonant|rhotic]])
*N is a [[nasal consonant]]
*S is a [[peripheral consonant]]
*h is a [[glottal consonant]].

Such complex codas are not unusual, and all combinations are enumerated as follows (words and translations taken from the dictionary<ref>Evans, Merlan & Tukumba (2004)</ref>).

===Phonological processes===
Dalabon has a pattern of eliding unstressed vowels and unstressed syllables. For example, the word /'cabale/ 'shoulder blade' is often realized as ['cable].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fletcher |first1=Janet |last2=Evans |first2=Nicholas |title=An acoustic phonetic analysis of intonational prominence in two Australian languages |journal=Journal of the International Phonetic Association |date=2002 |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=123–140 |doi=10.1017/S0025100302001019 |s2cid=144244382 }}</ref>

===Prosody===
The location of phrasal stress in Dalabon appears one or two peaks with an initial rise into the first peak at the left edge of the constituent and a final fall at the right edge of the constituent.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Ross |first1=Belinda |title=The phonological/grammatical mismatch in the Dalabon word: a phonetic study |date=2003 |hdl=11343/35879 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The diminutive [[enclitic]] ''=wurd'' is derived from noun ''wurd'' 'woman's child', its reduplication ''wurdurd'' means 'child'. 
''wurd'' can attach to most word classes and functions in 3 ways of meaning: to denote small objects, to add emotional connotations and to serve as pragmatic functions (especially for interactional softening). ===Syntax===
Dalabon is a head-marking language. Dalabon has limited use of subordinate clauses, but it has a distinctive subordination strategy, which is to attach pronominal prefixes to the verb, and marked verbs are used for subordinate clause functions<ref name="Evans, N. 2006"/>
